name: PT Bank Mandiri (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Mandiri: a capital-constrained franchise priced for a permanent downcycle
frontmatter.summary: We initiate Bank Mandiri at BUY with a target of Rp5,731, a 72.4% total return. The bank earns about a fifth of book, pays out four-fifths of it and trades at 1.1x book, capitalising a permanent return of about fourteen percent against the 19.6% our forecast delivers. Growth is now capped by capital, not demand. A bear case that adopts the market discount rate values the shares at today's price.
thesis: The BSI deconsolidation is a perimeter change rather than an earnings loss: Mandiri keeps 51.5% of BSI through equity accounting, so the parent profit path survives, and 9M26 pro-forma net profit still grew 20.7% year on year [S4][S2].
The 9M26 run-rate already delivers the guide, with NIM at 4.4%, cost-to-income at 38.0% and cost of credit at 0.6% inside the bands management maintained in October [S2].

Capital, not demand, is now the binding constraint: a 18.4% bank-only capital ratio against an internal target of 18.0% to 20.0% and a 79.0% payout funds loan growth of about 6.0%, not the guidance band [S2][S10].

The variant view is in the asset-quality description: loans at risk of 6.8% sit against a 1.0% gross NPL and coverage of 235.0%, so we normalise credit cost to 0.7% rather than hold the 9M26 charge [S2].

Our justified P/B is 1.8x against a traded 1.1x on a 12.8% cost of equity that sits inside the house band; the gap is the whole call, and it is a statement about the Indonesian discount rate rather than about a misread perimeter [S0][S11].

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Bank Mandiri with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of Rp5,731, a total return of 72.4% from the Rp3,610 price at which the shares trade, made up of 58.8% of capital appreciation and a gross dividend of Rp494 a share [S0]. The target is the probability-weighted average of three scenarios built around a base case, in which the bear case — the market's own discount rate applied to our earnings path — values the shares at roughly today's price [S2].

The price implies a permanent downcycle. At 1.1x book on an FY2026E return on equity of 19.6%, and on our 12.8% cost of equity, the market is capitalising a going-concern return on equity of about fourteen percent, against the 23.1% the bank earned on a bank-only basis in FY2025 and the 19.6% our own forecast produces [S3][S0]. Part of that discount has nothing to do with Mandiri. In October 2026 the IHSG fell 16.7% to close at 5,057 and foreign investors recorded IDR16.88tn of net sales after MSCI opened a consultation on reclassifying Indonesia from emerging to standalone market status, citing accessibility, shareholding transparency and market governance [S11]. Every Indonesian bank was repriced by that event, and our call should be read as a statement about the required return the market is charging the sector, not as a claim that the market misread an accounting note [S11].

Our judgement is that the operating franchise is intact and that the return being demanded is above the one the business earns. The pro-forma accounts make the first half of that case: 9M26 net profit of IDR45.53tn on a pro-forma ex-BSI base of IDR37.73tn is 20.7% higher year on year, with the margin at 4.4%, the cost-to-income ratio at 38.0% and cost of credit at 0.6% inside the guidance management maintained in October [S2]. The second half is arithmetic: a 12.8% required return against a franchise earning about a fifth of book with most of its funding in customer deposits is a gap that stays wide even after a bear case [S2][S0].

What we do not assume is that the balance sheet can grow its way out of the discount. The 79.0% payout [S10] on a return on equity near a fifth retains only a fifth of profit, and the bank-only capital adequacy ratio of 18.4% already sits at the bottom of management's own 18.0% to 20.0% target [S2]. We therefore model loans at 6.0% in FY2027E and FY2028E and 5.5% thereafter, below the 9.0% to 11.0% band the company guides for FY2026, and we hold that lower growth for a decade [S2]. The dividend, not the loan book, is the mechanism through which the shareholder is paid while the discount persists.

Three things move the value from here. The first is the cost of funds: bank-only deposit costs rose to 2.3% in the third quarter and the statutory reserve release is expected to relieve the pressure, which is an assumption about deposit competition rather than about policy alone [S2][S9]. The second is asset quality: loans at risk of 6.8% against a 1.0% gross NPL and coverage of 235.0% is the part of the book that decides whether a 0.6% charge stays near the middle of the guidance range [S2]. The third is the discount rate itself: the re-rating from 1.1x to 1.8x is the larger part of the expected return, and the dividend contributes about a fifth of it, which is why we describe the dividend as compensation for waiting rather than as the floor under the call [S0].

Bank Mandiri is the largest Indonesian bank by assets and the anchor of the state-owned banking group, operating a universal franchise that spans corporate and institutional banking, commercial and small-business lending, microfinance, consumer lending and wealth management [S3]. The bank runs a nationwide distribution network of branches, automated teller machines and electronic data capture terminals, and it reaches retail customers through the Livin application and its merchant and agent platforms, which the annual report presents as the delivery channel for the ecosystem strategy rather than as a standalone digital product [S3]. Group employment was 40,465 people at the last count carried in the pack [S0].

The lending mix is weighted toward corporate and commercial exposure, with the corporate book leading the current cycle and ecosystem-linked small, micro and consumer lending growing more slowly [S8]. Funding is built on current and savings accounts, which reached IDR1,186.06tn on a bank-only basis at the end of FY2025, and the bank describes the CASA franchise as the anchor of its cost-of-funds advantage [S3]. The ratio table shows a CASA ratio of 71.9% and a loan-to-deposit ratio of 91.2% at 9M26, both lower than a year earlier as deposit competition took its toll [S2]. Non-interest income comes from fees and commissions, treasury and securities gains, insurance distribution and the subsidiary businesses, and it is close to a third of total operating income on the 9M26 pro-forma run-rate [S2].

The defining corporate event of the period is the loss of control over Bank Syariah Indonesia. The state enterprises governance body revoked the special power of attorney it had granted Mandiri over the Series A Dwiwarna share and granted a new one to Danantara Asset Management, which under the applicable accounting standards removed Mandiri control from the first day of February 2026 [S4]. Mandiri derecognised BSI net assets of IDR49.42tn and non-controlling interest of IDR23.84tn, retains a 51.5% stake and now accounts for the company under the equity method, recognising its share of profit in the income statement [S4]. That description comes from the deconsolidation note in the interim financial statements rather than from secondary commentary, and it is the note the rest of this report relies on [S4].

The remaining group is a set of wholly or majority-owned subsidiaries that support the bank rather than compete with it: Bank Mandiri Taspen in commercial and pension-linked banking, the consumer finance arm, the insurance distribution joint ventures and the securities and remittance businesses [S4]. Consolidated minority interest fell with the deconsolidation, and the minority share of profit fell to about a thirtieth of group profit, which mechanically lifts parent earnings per unit of group profit without any change in the underlying economics [S4].

Ownership and control sit with the state. At 9M26 the Government of Indonesia held 52.0% of the shares through Danantara, the Indonesia Investment Authority held 8.0% and foreign investors held 26.6%, while the Republic retains the single Series A Dwiwarna share and the controlling-shareholder status [S2]. That mix is the governance fact that matters for a minority holder: the state controls the bank, the sovereign wealth body is both a shareholder and the recipient of the BSI voting power, and the foreign institutional base is large enough to be the marginal price-setter but not large enough to influence policy [S2][S4].

Competitively, Mandiri is the leader in wholesale and corporate banking among the state banks and a strong challenger in consumer and microfinance, where the private banks and the digital lenders set the pace [S3]. Its advantage is relationship depth with large corporates and the state-linked supply chains around them, which produces low-cost transactional deposits and a pipeline of cross-sell into cash management, trade finance and treasury [S3]. The strategy management describes is to defend that core while pushing ecosystem lending into the supply chains of corporate clients and digitising the cost to serve, which is the logic that took the cost-to-income ratio to 38.0% in 9M26 [S2].

Indonesian banking is a large, concentrated and regulated industry in which the state banks, the large private banks and the sharia banks compete for a deposit pool that grows with nominal output. Credit growth has run ahead of deposit growth through the current cycle, which is why the system loan-to-deposit ratio has tightened and why liquidity, rather than capital, has been the binding constraint on growth for most players; Mandiri is the exception, where capital is now the constraint and liquidity is not [S2][S3].

The Indonesian banking system has consolidated around a small number of large groups since the Asian financial crisis, when the sector was recapitalised and the weaker institutions were merged or closed. Entry is restricted by minimum capital and by the licensing regime, so competition is fought on funding cost, distribution and digital service quality rather than on the number of institutions. State ownership gives the largest banks access to government deposits and to infrastructure and commodity-related lending that private banks reach less easily.

The regulatory backdrop is supportive on liquidity and unhelpful on margin. Bank Indonesia cut the rupiah statutory reserve requirement for conventional banks to 7.0%, phased from the first day of November 2026, and the heads of the state banks publicly welcomed the release of liquidity it implies for lending [S9]. The same review kept the policy rate on hold at 5.8%, and the house macro deck carries that rate unchanged through FY2027E with real growth near 5.3% and inflation near 3.3% [S0]. A reserve cut is a liquidity and volume lever, not a margin lever: it lowers the share of deposits that must sit at the central bank, but it does not change the price the bank pays for those deposits, and our margin assumption treats it accordingly [S9].

Competition for deposits is the central competitive fact. The large state banks all reported rising deposit costs through the year as they competed for time deposits, and Mandiri bank-only cost of deposits rose to 2.3% in the third quarter before stabilising in the monthly data [S2]. Loan pricing improved at the same time, with bank-only loan yields rising to 7.0% as existing loans repriced, so the net interest margin compressed by less than the rise in funding costs would imply [S2]. The competitive set is the other state banks and the largest private banks in corporate and commercial lending, the consumer-finance companies and the digital banks in micro and retail, and the sharia banks in the segments where religion is a purchase criterion [S9][S3].

The sector was repriced twice in the past year, once for the cycle and once for the index. The IHSG fell 16.7% in October 2026 to 5,057 after MSCI published its consultation on reclassifying Indonesia as a standalone market, and the financial services authority reported IDR16.88tn of net foreign selling in the same month, with the bond index also lower [S11]. MSCI framed the consultation around accessibility, shareholding transparency and market governance, which are index-construction questions rather than earnings questions [S11]. For a bank trading at 1.1x book with a 23.1% bank-only return on equity, the distinction matters: an index-driven de-rating can push a share price below the value of its cash flows without saying anything about the loan book, and it can persist for as long as the classification question is open [S11][S3].

The moat is real but narrower than the balance sheet suggests. The transactional deposit franchise and the corporate relationships are durable, because switching a cash-management mandate is costly for a large corporate treasurer, and the state-linked flow of payroll, pension and infrastructure payments reinforces it [S3]. Against that, the bank competes for the same deposits as its peers, its loan pricing is set by a market that includes cheaper-funded private banks, and its consumer franchise is smaller than the leaders [S3]. We would characterise the moat as moderate: enough to earn a return on equity well above the cost of equity through the cycle, not enough to defend a margin against a sustained funding shock.

On the five forces, buyer power is high in corporate lending and moderate in retail; supplier power is high in deposits, which is where the current margin pressure comes from; the threat of new entrants is low in corporate banking and moderate in digital retail lending; substitutes are growing in payments and wealth, where non-bank platforms take fee pools; and rivalry is intense but disciplined, because the large banks price for profitability rather than volume, as the profitability-first language and the loan-growth guidance in the deck show [S2]. The external influences that matter most are the rupiah and the sovereign yield, through the cost of equity and through the funding market; commodity prices, through the credit quality of the resource-related corporate book; and fiscal policy, through state deposits and infrastructure lending [S3].

The reported history is a bank that compounded its balance sheet through the last cycle. Gross loans and sharia financing rose from IDR1,623.22tn at the end of FY2024 to IDR1,849.97tn at the end of FY2025, and customer deposits rose from IDR1,446.23tn to IDR1,816.90tn over the same period, which took the bank-only loan-to-deposit ratio to 88.9% [S7][S3]. Net interest income on the data pack conventional definition rose from IDR88.92tn to IDR91.57tn, and non-interest income from IDR45.88tn to IDR48.60tn, producing pre-tax profit of IDR76.42tn and parent profit of IDR56.29tn [S7].

The perimeter is the thing to understand before reading any year-on-year comparison. The pack interest line is conventional interest income less interest expense, so it excludes the sharia margin income that BSI earned; the audited income statement shows net interest and sharia income of a materially larger figure that includes it [S7]. When BSI left the consolidation the group lost BSI sharia margin income and the BSI cost base together, which is why the FY2025A cost-to-income line in our model of 48.2% is not comparable with the 9M26 figure of 38.0%: the first is struck on conventional income that never carried the sharia revenue, the second on the ex-BSI perimeter management now guides [S7][S2]. Parent profit is unaffected in substance because equity accounting still recognises Mandiri share of BSI profit, and the minority interest that used to absorb the other part of it is gone; the pro-forma comparison in the results deck, which restates the prior year on the same perimeter, shows the effect [S4][S2].

Margins have compressed and we do not assume they recover. The bank-only net interest margin was 4.6% in FY2025, and on the ex-BSI consolidated basis it moved from 4.5% in FY2025 to 4.4% in 9M26 as deposit costs rose and the loan book repriced only partially [S3][S2]. We hold 4.3% for FY2026E and for every year after it, including the terminal year, which is a deliberate rejection of the margin-recovery trade: the house macro deck keeps the policy rate at 5.8% through FY2027E and its stance on rate-sensitive Indonesian bank margins is to avoid exactly that trade, and the company's own deposit cost rose in every quarter of the year [S0][S2]. A flat margin is the assumption a sceptic would defend: the maintained guidance range is a narrow band either side of it, and we take the middle and stop there [S2].

Costs are the most credible part of the equity story. Management lowered the FY2026 cost-to-income guidance band and delivered 38.0% in 9M26, driven by digital channel migration, automation in back-office operations and network discipline [S2]. Our model holds that level for FY2026E and drifts to 37.0% by FY2030E, which is a mild efficiency assumption rather than a heroic one: it keeps the operating cost base growing more slowly than revenue without assuming a restructuring management has not announced [S2].

Asset quality is where we are least comfortable, and it is described here with the current numbers. Gross NPL is low at 1.0% on the ex-BSI consolidated basis in 9M26, but coverage of 235.0% is down from the 252.6% the bank reported on a bank-only basis at the end of FY2025, and loans at risk rose to 6.8% on restructured performing loans against a cost of credit of 0.6% [S2][S3]. A coverage ratio that has fallen while the at-risk book has risen is the direction of travel a credit analyst should care about, not the absolute NPL, which is flattered by the restructured classification [S2]. We therefore forecast credit cost at 0.7% for FY2026E and 0.7% from FY2028E, above the current charge and inside the guidance band, and we show the value sensitivity to it below [S2][S7].

Capital is comfortable, and it is also the constraint that sets the growth path. The bank-only capital adequacy ratio was 19.4% at the end of FY2025 and 18.4% at 9M26, against an internal target of 18.0% to 20.0% for the bank-only ratio [S3][S2]. We calibrate risk-weighted assets at 0.94 times gross loans, a ratio set so that FY2026E book equity over the ex-BSI loan book reproduces the reported 18.4%; it sits above the deck's raw risk-weight density because regulatory capital deducts the equity-accounted BSI stake and goodwill that book equity still carries, so the model's capital line should be read as the trajectory of the reported bank-only ratio rather than as a regulatory calculation [S2]. On that basis the capital ratio moves from 18.4% in FY2026E to 18.0% in FY2029E and 18.1% in the terminal year, never below the floor of the internal target, because loans grow at roughly the rate of retained equity rather than faster [S2]. That is the difference between this forecast and one in which the return on equity rises because the balance sheet is being levered: the model's return on equity stays between 19.5% and 20.0% for the whole forecast, and the terminal value is discounted on the return the bank earns today rather than on a leverage-driven drift [S2]. Liquidity is supported by the CASA franchise and by the reserve-requirement release, and the deposit growth we forecast keeps the loan-to-deposit ratio near 94.1% throughout, below the management ceiling [S2][S9].

Capital return is predictable and the payout is the binding constraint on growth. The book-year 2025 dividend of IDR44.47tn was set at the 79.0% payout we carry, an IDR6.16tn interim was paid for book year 2026, and 91.75 million shares were repurchased for the employee ownership programme rather than cancelled, leaving the share count unchanged [S10]. One mechanical point on the model: the dividend line is on a calendar-cash basis, so each year carries the prior book year's final dividend plus the current year's interim, which is why the model's historical payout ratio reads high against the book-year ratio the company discloses; the forward 79.0% is the book-year payout, and it is the same ratio applied one year forward rather than a cut [S10][S2].

Our forecast is a smaller reported balance sheet carrying slightly more profit. We have FY2026E loans of IDR1,740.08tn, deposits of IDR1,849.60tn, net interest income of IDR93.61tn, non-interest income of IDR46.56tn, pre-tax profit of IDR75.24tn and parent profit of IDR58.35tn, which is 3.7% earnings per share growth to Rp625 and a return on equity of 19.6% [S2]. The loan line is -5.9% on the reported perimeter because BSI leaves the base; on the bank-only book the comparison is different, with credit of IDR1,605.84tn at 9M26 up 7.3% year to date [S2][S4]. We anchor on the year-to-date figure rather than the year-on-year rate published alongside it, because the year-to-date figure is what management guides against and what reconciles to the balance sheet [S2][S8]. By FY2027E the reported series is clean and grows at 6.0% [S2][S4]. The base case sits just under four percent below the annualised 9M26 run-rate, because we provision above the annualised charge and hold a flat margin; on the pro-forma base the company grew 20.7% in 9M26, and our FY2026E assumes that momentum slows rather than reverses [S2].

On earnings quality we carry one structural flag and one optical one. The structural flag is the restructured-loan book: loans at risk of 6.8% against coverage of 235.0% means reported profit depends on the assumption that restructured borrowers cure rather than default, and a migration of that book into NPL would raise the charge without changing the underlying franchise [S2][S3]. The optical flag is the equity-accounted BSI income: it is real cash earnings once distributed, but it sits below the operating line, carries no consolidation of the BSI balance sheet, and will make reported revenue growth look lower than economic growth [S4]. We see no evidence of the manipulation-class flags that matter more, namely a gap between provisioning and write-offs that flatters profit, related-party revenue inflation or a change of accounting estimate that lifts earnings, and the auditor issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 accounts [S7].

A bank is valued on the relationship between the return it earns on equity and the return its shareholders require, so the primary method is a justified price-to-book that capitalises the sustainable spread between the two, with a residual income model and a dividend discount model as cross-checks that share the same cost of equity and terminal growth [S3]. The method set suits a regulated, capital-constrained, dividend-paying lender better than a free-cash-flow model, because a bank cash flow is not a meaningful concept once loan growth and regulatory capital are endogenous to the business.

The cost of equity is 12.8%, and the build has to be argued against the house band rather than simply described. The engine starts from the Indonesian sovereign yield of 7.4% less the default spread of 1.6%, plus a beta of 0.90 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, which produces a rate below the band the house method pins for Indonesian rupiah equities [S0]. We therefore add a 0.95% premium to land at 12.8%, inside the band and above the rate the same book uses for the premium private bank, because that bank is cheaper-funded and more profitable than Mandiri on every operating line: a higher net interest margin, a lower cost-to-income ratio and a less policy-exposed shareholder register [S2][S0]. There is no case for giving Mandiri a lower discount rate than the premium franchise, and we do not [S0]. The bank has no financial debt in the capital structure we model, so the cost of equity is the cost of capital and the weights are trivial; there is no leverage adjustment and no debt tax shield to argue about.

The primary method values the equity at Rp5,650 per share. It takes the sustainable ROE of 19.6% that the first three forecast years average, a terminal growth of 4.2%, and applies the warranted multiple of 1.8x to the book value per share at the latest balance sheet. The sustainable ROE is not an assumption bolted on: it is the output of the margin, cost and credit-cost path in the financial section, it is close to the 23.1% bank-only return the group reported for FY2025, and it does not rise through the forecast [S3]. Terminal growth is set at 4.2%, which is what a return on equity of about a fifth and a 79.0% payout can fund from retained earnings, not the nominal growth rate of the economy; the house deck's real growth plus inflation path is a macro forecast the bank cannot fund at this payout without a capital raise, so the lower figure is the capital-consistent cap and is the one the model obeys [S0][S2][S10].

The cross-checks agree and now sit close to the primary. The residual-income model values the shares at Rp6,225, 10.2% above the primary, and the dividend discount model values them at Rp6,325, 11.9% above the primary, both because they carry the full ten-year path rather than a three-year average of the return on equity [S3]. The residual-income value is the larger because it credits the bank with the equity it accumulates, and the dividend model is close to it because the payout returns most of that equity to shareholders each year. We weight the primary at half the total, the residual-income model at three tenths and the dividend model at two tenths, because the primary is the method whose inputs are all things the company has reported, whereas the cross-checks depend on the shape of the terminal years [S3].

The sensitivity table ranks the levers the other way round from the intuition that a long-duration equity claim is a bet on the discount rate. A one-point move in credit cost or in the net interest margin changes the target by more than a one-point move in the cost of equity or in terminal growth, because the earnings base is what the multiple is applied to, and a bank with a flat margin converts a credit or funding shock straight into book value [S2]. The call is therefore an operating bet first and a rate bet second: the margin holding near the 9M26 level and the charge staying inside the guidance band are what protect the value, and the discount-rate normalisation is the part of the return we do not control and do not need [S2].

The peer set is the cross-check that any warranted multiple has to survive. Mandiri's warranted multiple of 1.8x should be, and is, below the multiple the market pays for the premium franchise listed in the table, because Mandiri earns a lower margin, runs a higher cost ratio and prices more credit risk than that competitor [S2][S0]. What the table also shows is that the entire listed bank set trades between roughly half of book and two and a quarter times book, with the median below book, including banks whose capital and credit quality are not in question [S0]. A framework that marks every one of them above its traded price is making a sector-wide claim about the Indonesian discount rate rather than a stock-specific claim about Mandiri, and we state that plainly rather than dressing it up as a mispricing the company can close by operating better [S0][S11].

What the current price implies is the mirror image of our conclusion. At 1.1x book the market is capitalising a permanent return on equity of about fourteen percent, well below the 23.1% the bank earned on a bank-only basis in FY2025 [S3][S0]. To justify that on our cost of equity the bank would have to lose several points of sustainable margin or run credit cost permanently above the top of its own guidance, and neither is in the evidence [S2]. The reverse reading is that the market is applying a country and governance discount that our method already captures through the country risk premium and through the premium we add to reach the house band; if that discount is permanent, our target is too high by the whole of the re-rating, which is exactly what the bear case values [S11][S0].

The largest risk is a funding shock. Deposits are the scarce input in the current cycle, bank-only cost of deposits rose to 2.3% in the third quarter, and a renewed competition for time deposits would compress the margin faster than loan repricing can offset it [S2]. Likelihood is moderate and impact is high, because the whole valuation rests on a sustained margin near the middle of the guidance range; the mitigation is the CASA franchise and the reserve-requirement release, which give the bank cheaper marginal funding than most competitors [S9][S3].

The second risk is asset quality. Loans at risk of 6.8% are concentrated in restructured performing loans and coverage of 235.0% is adequate rather than generous, having fallen from the prior year's level [S2][S3]. If a meaningful part of that book migrates into NPL, credit cost would move from the middle of the guidance band toward the top and the earnings base would fall; likelihood is moderate and impact is moderate, because the bank has provisioned through a full cycle and the corporate book is not concentrated in a single commodity [S3].

Regulatory and political risk is the third. The state is the controlling shareholder at 52.0% through Danantara, and decisions on dividends, subsidised lending programmes, the BSI stake and the role of the bank in national projects are taken with policy objectives that may not maximise the value of the minority shares [S2][S4]. The precedent is the transfer of BSI voting power to Danantara Asset Management, which changed the consolidation perimeter without a change in economic ownership and without a minority vote [S4]. Likelihood is high that policy flows continue and impact is moderate, bounded by the size of the institutional base and by the capital position.

The fourth risk is governance at BSI itself. Mandiri no longer controls the bank whose profit it now equity-accounts, and the arrangement that produced the change is a live issue for how BSI is run, how its capital is allocated and whether Mandiri share of its profit is paid out [S4]. A change in BSI dividend policy or a capital raise that dilutes the stake would hit the equity-accounted income directly, and the market has no operating lever to influence it.

Liquidity and market risk are second order for the equity but first order for the trading pattern. The shares turned over IDR651.1bn a day over the last three months, which is deep enough for the position to be investable at scale, and the price sits near the low of its range over the past year at Rp3,360 against a high of Rp5,375 [S0]. The rupiah is the transmission channel: a weaker currency raises the sovereign yield, lifts the cost of equity and pressures the funding market at the same time, and the house deck carries the exchange rate at Rp18,004/USD and the dollar index at 102.2 [S0]. The MSCI consultation is the second channel, and it operates through flows rather than through fundamentals [S11].

The scenarios are built to give the market its own case rather than to bracket the price. The bear case at Rp3,531 is the market's valuation of the bank: a higher cost of equity at the top of the house band, a margin compressed below anything the bank has reported in this cycle, a credit charge through the top of the guidance range, and a payout cut to defend the capital ratio, which is the combination that produces a return on equity near the one today's price implies [S2][S0]. It values the shares at about Rp3,349 before the dividend, essentially today's price, so the downside in this stock is the loss of the waiting return rather than a second de-rating. The base case at Rp6,226 holds the 9M26 run-rate, the flat margin, the normalised charge and the payout policy, and the bull case at Rp6,942 assumes the funding cycle turns, the charge returns to the guidance floor and the risk premium unwinds to the bottom of the house band [S2][S9][S0].

The bull is deliberately constrained by evidence rather than by symmetry. Its credit-cost relief stops at the 0.6% floor of the guidance range because the charge has not been below that level in either of the last two years, and its margin recovery stops at the top of the maintained guidance range because that is the highest margin management has guided to [S2][S7]. The bear has no such floor, which is why the two tails are not mirror images in size, and we set the probabilities at 50% for the base and 25% in each tail rather than pretending to a precision the exercise does not have [S2].

The signposts that would change our view are specific. A bank-only cost of deposits above its third-quarter level for two consecutive quarters would tell us the funding advantage has gone; a rise in gross NPL above the current level with coverage falling further would tell us the restructured book is seasoning; and a dividend below the payout we forecast would tell us the state is prioritising capital or policy lending over the minority [S2][S10]. On the other side, a credit-cost print near the bottom of the guidance band with loans at risk falling, or an MSCI decision that removes the classification question, would justify moving towards the bull case [S2][S11].

Ownership and control are concentrated in the state. The Government of Indonesia holds 52.0% through Danantara, the Indonesia Investment Authority holds 8.0% and foreign investors hold 26.6%, while the Republic retains the single Series A Dwiwarna share and the controlling-shareholder status [S2]. The institutional base is large enough that the shares clear the index eligibility tests on liquidity, but it is not large enough to constrain a shareholder that can change the perimeter of the bank, as it did with BSI, without needing minority consent [S4][S2]. In a market where MSCI has cited shareholding transparency as a reason to question Indonesia's classification, the ownership disclosure in the results deck is the relevant standard and it is complete at the level of the register [S11][S2].

Related-party exposure is large and structural rather than incidental, and it can be quantified. The audited accounts disclose related-party loans and sharia receivables of IDR402.85tn against a gross loan book of IDR1,849.97tn, which is more than a fifth of lending to entities connected to the state or to the group [S7]. On the funding side, related-party demand deposits of IDR197.25tn and time deposits of IDR206.27tn together account for more than a fifth of the IDR1,816.90tn deposit base [S7]. That is the disclosure the earnings-quality framework asks for as a percentage of the total, and it is high by the standards of a private bank. The disclosure is complete and the lending-limit compliance is clean, with no reported breach of the legal lending limit to related or third parties in the annual report ratio table [S3]. The risk is price risk rather than disclosure risk: related-party lending can be priced or restructured for policy reasons, and the state is both the counterparty and the controller [S7][S2].

The auditor issued an unmodified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts, with the impairment of loans and sharia receivables identified as the key audit matter and with the audit work set out in the report [S7]. We found no qualification, emphasis of matter or restatement in the accounts we used. The 9M26 interim accounts were reviewed and the BSI deconsolidation was disclosed in full, including the derecognised net assets and the equity-accounted treatment, which is the transparency standard we would want on a transaction of that size [S4].

The dividend record is strong and the policy is explicit. The bank paid IDR44.47tn for book year 2025, declared an interim of IDR6.16tn for book year 2026, and repurchased 91.75 million shares for the employee programme rather than cancelling them, which keeps the share count and the per-share dividend intact [S10]. We read the 79.0% payout we forecast as the state preferred way of extracting cash from the bank, and we see the dividend as more secure than a buyback because it is the mechanism the controlling shareholder has actually used. That is also why a payout cut is the most direct way the controlling shareholder could hurt the minority, and why it is one of the shocks in the bear case [S10][S2].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones typical of a large Indonesian bank: financed emissions in the power, palm oil, mining and cement sectors, and a transition-finance opportunity as the corporate book reallocates toward renewable and downstream processing. The annual report sets out the sustainability framework and the green-financing commitments, and the governance structure places sustainability under the board rather than under a marketing function [S3]. The social and governance dimensions are dominated by the state-ownership question: board composition, related-party pricing and the treatment of minority shareholders in perimeter transactions matter more to an equity investor than the quality of the environmental disclosure.

The near-term catalysts are dated and mostly policy-driven. The FY2026 dividend declaration and the guidance for FY2027 in December are the first test of whether the state keeps the payout at the level we forecast [S10]. The MSCI consultation decision is the second, and it is the one that decides whether the sector discount we describe is a permanent feature of the market or a temporary flow event [S11]. The FY2026 audited accounts at the end of January are the first full year on the ex-BSI perimeter and will confirm whether the equity-accounted BSI income and the restated cost base behave as we model [S2][S4]. The Bank Indonesia board meeting in February sets the liquidity backdrop for the next lending season before the annual meeting approves the book-year 2026 dividend [S9][S10].

Between updates we monitor a short list of operating variables. The bank-only cost of deposits and the loan yield together determine the margin, so we track both monthly against the 7.0% yield and the 2.3% cost of deposits we last saw [S2]. Loans at risk and coverage are the asset-quality tripwires, with gross NPL at 1.0% and coverage at 235.0% the levels to beat [S2]. Loan growth against the capital-funded path, the cost-to-income ratio against the 38.0% delivered in 9M26, the bank-only capital ratio against the 18.0% floor of the internal target, and the equity-accounted BSI contribution are the remaining four, and a change in any of them is what would move us off this view [S2][S4].

bear.narrative: The market is right and the de-rating is structural: deposit competition and the balance-of-payments regime cap the margin, the restructured book seasons into the charge, the risk premium settles at the top of the house band, and the state cuts the payout to defend an 18% CAR while lending slows.

bull.narrative: The rupiah stabilises: the GWM cut and CASA growth hold the margin at the guidance top, the restructured book cures and credit cost returns to the bottom of the guidance band, the risk premium falls back to the house band floor, and the state lifts the payout as capital stops being the constraint on growth.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs NIM and credit cost
12-month value vs cost of equity and terminal growth

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is a perimeter step, not a demand call: BSI was deconsolidated from 1 February 2026 (net assets Rp49.4tn derecognised) [S4], so the reported FY2025A loan base of Rp1,850tn falls to about Rp1,740tn at Dec-26E, which is the Sep-26 ex-BSI book of Rp1,694tn [S2] plus one quarter at the 9M26 run-rate. From FY2027E growth is capital-constrained, not guidance-led: the bank-only CAR was 18.4% at 9M26 against an internal target of 18.0-20.0% [S2], and the residual 21% retention on a ~20% ROE funds roughly 5.5-6% of RWA growth, so 6.0% in FY2027-28 and 5.5% thereafter is what the 79% payout [S10] can carry without a capital raise. The 9-11% guidance [S2] is a FY2026 number: the bank-only book is already up 7.26% year to date [S2], and lending faster than retained capital would take the CAR through its own floor without a payout cut.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: Same perimeter effect: BSI deposits leave the reported base, so FY2026E growth is only +1.8% even though third-party funds grew 4.5% year-to-date on the bank-only book to Sep-26 [S2]. From FY2027E deposits grow with loans so the loan-to-deposit ratio holds near 94%, inside the below-95% ceiling management targets [S2]; the GWM cut from 9% to 7% phased from 1 November 2026 adds lending headroom without deposit growth [S9].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Calibration constant, not a balance-sheet ratio: 1.2044 is the multiple at which the model's average earning-asset base reproduces the NII run-rate implied by management's 4.43% 9M26 NIM [S2] on the FY2025A bank-only asset base of Rp2,228tn [S3]. It is held flat because the loan-to-securities mix is stable in the deck [S2].

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the 9M26 run-rate: NIM fell from 4.70% in 1Q26 to 4.43% by 9M26 as deposit costs rose every quarter to 2.34% in 3Q26 [S2], and management kept the 4.3-4.5% guidance [S2]. No recovery is assumed: the house macro deck carries the policy rate at 5.75% through FY2027E and its stance on rate-sensitive Indonesian bank margins is to avoid the NIM-recovery trade [S0], and the deck series show deposit costs still rising into 3Q26 [S2]. 4.33% is held flat for the forecast and set as the terminal margin, so the model earns the observed run-rate rather than a GWM-driven improvement; the GWM release is treated as a liquidity and volume lever [S9], not a margin lever.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Fee income tracks the smaller book: FY2026E falls 4.2% because BSI fee income leaves the consolidated base with the deconsolidation [S4]; the 9M26 ex-BSI run-rate is about Rp35tn against Rp48.6tn reported for FY2025. From FY2027E fees grow at 6-7%, a little faster than loans on digital and ecosystem transaction volumes but slower than the 8% taken before, in line with the recurring fee growth management reports and the shallower lending path [S2].

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Management lowered FY2026 guidance to 37-39% and delivered 38.0% in 9M26 [S2]; the base case holds 38.0% for FY2026E and drifts to 37.0% as digital channels and back-office automation take cost out, the efficiency path management describes [S2].

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: 9M26 cost of credit was 0.63% and FY2025 0.60% [S2][S7]; guidance is 0.6-0.8% [S2]. The base case takes 0.65% for FY2026E and normalises to 0.70% because loans at risk rose 93bp QoQ to 6.76% on restructured performing loans [S2], which keeps provisioning above the current charge without assuming a cycle turn.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: Set to zero from FY2026E: the FY2025A positive balance is the sharia margin income that sat outside the pack's conventional interest line and left the group with BSI on 1 February 2026 [S4]. No recurring non-operating item is assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025A effective rate was 19.7% (tax Rp15.1tn on pre-tax profit Rp76.4tn) [S7]; held flat, with no change in the corporate rate assumed.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority profit fell to about 3.3% of group net profit in 9M26 from 8.4% in FY2025 because BSI's non-controlling interest left the consolidation [S4]; 3.4% is held, reflecting the remaining subsidiaries (Bank Mandiri Taspen, MTF, AXA Mandiri).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The book-year 2025 dividend of Rp44.47tn is 79% of FY2025 parent profit [S10], and a Rp6.16tn interim was paid for book year 2026 [S10]; 79% is held, inside the 60-85% SOE range, and is the payout the state has actually taken in the last two book years [S2]. It is also the binding constraint on growth: at a ~20% ROE it retains only about a fifth of profit, which is why the loan path slows to what an 18.0-20.0% internal CAR target can fund [S2]. The bear case values the state cutting it to 60% to defend capital [S2].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No change: the 91.75m shares bought back were transferred to the employee ownership programme, leaving the 93.3bn share count intact [S10].

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: Calibration constant, not a regulatory calculation: 0.94 is the multiple at which FY2026E book equity over the ex-BSI loan book reproduces the reported bank-only CAR of 18.4% at 9M26 [S2]. It sits above the deck's raw risk-weight density because regulatory capital deducts the equity-accounted BSI stake and goodwill that book equity still carries; held flat, the model's capital ratio is therefore read as the trajectory of the reported ratio rather than as a regulatory CAR. The internal target of 18.0-20.0% bank-only CAR [S2] bounds loan growth to what retained earnings can fund.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 4.2%: the rate the model can fund from retained earnings. With a ~20% sustainable ROE and the 79% payout the company has actually paid [S10], retention funds ROE x (1 - payout) of about 4.3% of capital and therefore of loans — the internal CAR target of 18.0-20.0% [S2] makes that the binding constraint, not the macro nominal path. The house macro deck's nominal path (real growth 5.29% plus CPI 3.28%) is not fundable at this payout without a capital raise, so the lower figure is the capital-consistent cap rather than a macro forecast [S0].

challenges.challenge: CONTAMINATION. S3 (the 2025 Annual Report cited throughout) reproduces broker research: '17 November 2025 3. Verdhana BUY 6,000 ... BRIS ... following the planned transfer of BRIS's golden share from BMRI back to Danantara by end-2025. If deconsolidation occurs, BRIS would be accounted for as an associate rather than fully consolidated, resulting in broadly unchanged headline net profit for BMRI but lower reported NIM ... The impact on capital adequacy is expected to be limited'. That is a sell-side rating and target inside a cited source, and its conclusion is the report's own central thesis in §3 ('Parent profit is unaffected in substance because equity accounting still recognises Mandiri share of BSI profit'). The 163 stripped consensus sentences in S3 did not catch it.
challenges.answer: CONTAMINATION confirmed and quarantined. The p.50 Main Highlights page of S3 reproduces a broker BUY with a target and a second note on the BRIS deconsolidation, and its conclusion matches this report thesis. fund record now carries an exclusion note for that page, no claim in fund record, fund record or fund record rests on it, and the deconsolidation reasoning in sections 1 and 3 is sourced only to S4 Note 1g. Section 1 states explicitly that the description comes from the interim financial statements rather than from secondary commentary.

challenges.challenge: COE is 11.851% (rf 7.45% less default spread 1.62%, plus 0.90 x (4.23% mature ERP + 2.46% CRP)). VAL_BANKS pins COE at the 10y sovereign plus an IDR ERP of 5.0-6.0%, i.e. 12.45-13.45%, and any number outside the band must be argued. The report describes the build but never argues it against the band, and the same house book gives BBCA - the premium franchise - a COE of 12.45% while BMRI, BBNI and BBRI get 11.85%. There is no case for BMRI, a lower-NIM higher-CTI franchise than BBCA, carrying a lower discount rate. At 12.45% the justified P/B falls from 2.069x to about 1.92x and the primary value from Rp6,517 to about Rp6,055 (-7%), and the target to roughly Rp7,400.
challenges.answer: Accepted and rebuilt. valuation.coe_premium is now 0.0095, taking the cost of equity to 12.80%, inside the house band of 12.45-13.45% and 35bp above the 12.45% the same book uses for BCA. The premium is argued on franchise rather than asserted: a lower NIM, a higher cost-to-income ratio and 52.0% state ownership through Danantara. Section 4 states the build, the band and the BCA comparison explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The terminal ROE of 23.13% (FY2035E) is not sustainable: equity grows from Rp301.4tn to Rp511.3tn over FY2026-35 (6.0% a year) while loans grow from Rp1,740.1tn to Rp3,709.0tn (8.7% a year), so the model CAR falls from 21.1% to 16.8% and keeps falling in the terminal at roughly 3.5% a year (8% loan growth against 4.2% retained equity). Card VAL_BANKS #5 requires growth to be capital-constrained (g <= ROE x (1 - payout), bounded by CET1); the base case violates it, and the rising ROE the RI and DDM capitalise is a leverage artefact, not a franchise improvement. The terminal value is 55% of the residual-income value and 52% of the DDM. The car_est line is also flattered: 0.82 was backed out from group equity over the bank-only CAR, so the model shows 21.1% in FY2026E against the AR's 19.36% bank-only CAR, and the loans are group loans.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Growth is now capital-constrained: loans 6.0% in FY2027E and FY2028E, 5.5% in FY2029E and 5.0% thereafter, against retained earnings of about 4.2% of capital at the 79% payout. Risk-weight density is recalibrated to 0.94 so FY2026E book equity over the ex-BSI book reproduces the reported 18.4% bank-only capital ratio, and the path now runs 18.4% to 18.0% to 18.1% without breaching the 18.0-20.0% internal target. The return on equity stays between 19.5% and 20.0% for the whole forecast and does not rise, so the residual-income and dividend models no longer capitalise a leverage artefact. Terminal growth of 4.2% equals the sustainable ROE times retention.

challenges.challenge: The scenario set has no path in which the market is right. Bear Rp5,677 is +57% from Rp3,610, base Rp7,858 is +118%, bull Rp10,631 is +194%; every state of the world is a large gain. The bear shocks only credit cost (+60bp to 1.25%, above the 0.6-0.8% guidance), NIM (-40bp) and loan growth (-3pp); it does not shock COE, even though the report says the discount rate is a dominant lever, and it still leaves an implied ~15% ROE and a ~1.5x warranted P/B. The market-implied ROE of ~12.8% at the model's own COE is never given a probability. A distribution with no downside branch cannot support a 'most likely' claim; it is an artefact of shocking three operating variables and holding the discount rate fixed.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The scenario set now has a genuine downside branch and a cost-of-equity shock. The bear case shocks val.coe by 60bp to the top of the house band, the margin by 80bp, credit cost by 80bp and the payout by 15pp, and values the shares at Rp3,531 against the Rp3,610 price, on a return on equity near the 13.8% the market capitalises: it is the market-is-right scenario. Base is Rp6,226 and bull Rp6,942 at 25/50/25. All four shocks appear in both tails, with written symmetry justifications in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: The report treats the 13.7% dividend yield as 'the floor under the call' and 'the largest single component of the expected return', but it never tests whether the payout is fundable at the modelled growth. A 79% payout on a 19.6% ROE returns 15.5% of book a year while loans grow 9-11%; on the model's own numbers the CAR erodes throughout, so the state must either cut the payout, slow lending, or accept a thinner capital buffer. The state is the controlling shareholder and has already moved BSI's control without a minority vote; the report itself lists a dividend below forecast as a change-of-view signpost but does not value that state. It also calls the figure a 'net' yield when the modelled DPS is gross of the Indonesian dividend tax. And 13.7% of the 135.5% expected return is one tenth of it: the claim that the dividend is the largest component is arithmetically wrong (capital appreciation is 121.8%).
challenges.answer: Accepted on all three points. The payout is now tested: the bear case cuts it by 15pp to 64% to defend the capital ratio, and base-case loan growth is slowed to what a 79% payout can fund. The yield is labelled gross and section 3 explains the calendar-cash basis of the dividend line. The largest-component claim is removed: the report now says the re-rating is the larger part of the expected return and the dividend contributes about a fifth of it.

challenges.challenge: The house macro regime is balance_of_payments_pressure / CAUTIOUS with the explicit stance 'INDO rate-sensitive banks NIM: AVOID', bi_rate 5.75% through FY2027, usd_idr 18,350 and DXY 102.25. The report never cites or engages it, calls the regulatory backdrop 'supportive', and builds a NIM path that is flat-to-up. Nor does it use the deck's terminal drivers: the assumption basis says 4.0% growth is 'consistent with the macro deck's real growth and inflation path', but 5.29% real plus 3.28% CPI is 8.57% nominal, and the basis cites [S3], the annual report, which cannot supply a macro terminal cap. Separately, S9 says the GWM cut is 9% to 7% phased from 1 November 2026, not 'in two steps during the quarter' as §2 states.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report now cites the house macro deck directly: policy rate 5.75% through FY2027E, real growth 5.29%, inflation 3.28%, and the AVOID stance on the Indonesian bank NIM trade, which is why the margin is held flat at 4.33% for every year including the terminal year. The reserve requirement is described correctly as a cut to 7.0% phased from 1 November 2026. Terminal growth of 4.2% is set on a capital-consistent basis sourced to the ROE and the payout, not to the annual report, and the report states that the 8.57% nominal macro path is not fundable at this payout.

challenges.challenge: There is no peer cross-check anywhere in the report, although the house book has the comps. BMRI is marked at a warranted 2.07x book; BBCA - NIM 5.78%, CTI 30.7%, credit cost 0.80% - trades at 2.07x and is marked at 2.40x, while BMRI has NIM 4.33%, CTI 38.0% and credit cost 0.65%. On the house's own numbers BMRI's fair value multiple equals the market price of the better franchise, which is a relative-value statement the report never confronts. Worse, the whole house BANKS book is BUY: BBCA +26.7%, BBNI +88.7%, BBRI +109.9%, BMRI +135.5%, with peer P/Bs of 0.57-2.07x and a median of 0.87x. If the framework marks all six IDR banks at roughly twice their traded price, the 'market is wrong' argument is a sector-wide claim that needs a sector-wide defence, not a BMRI insight.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report now carries the peer table and states that the warranted 1.79x sits below the multiple the market pays for the premium franchise, because Mandiri runs a lower margin, a higher cost ratio and more credit risk. It also states that the entire listed bank set trades between roughly half of book and two and a quarter times book, with a median below book, so a framework that marks all of them above their traded prices is a sector-wide discount-rate claim rather than a Mandiri insight, and the bear case is where that shows up.

challenges.challenge: The report explains the 1.1x book as the market misreading the BSI deconsolidation ('the market appears to have read the perimeter change as a permanent loss of earning power') without a single piece of evidence for that causal claim. The house registry points the other way: the IHSG fell 38% in the year to 21 October 2026, MSCI opened a consultation on 15 October 2026 to move Indonesia to Standalone, index increases are frozen, and BMRI is down ~33% from its 52-week high. A sector-wide, index and macro-driven de-rating is at least as likely as a BMRI-specific misreading, and it would not be corrected by the company's operating performance. The report's own risk section notes the rupiah/sovereign-yield channel but does not connect it to the discount.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The unsourced claim that the market misread the perimeter is removed. The report attributes the de-rating to the index and macro channel with evidence: the IHSG fell 16.7% in October 2026 to 5,057 and foreign investors sold Rp16.88tn net after MSCI opened its standalone consultation on accessibility, shareholding transparency and governance grounds. S11 was fetched for this purpose and registered as a dated source. The report also sets out what would distinguish a company-specific mispricing from a sector de-rating, and adds the MSCI decision to the catalysts and to the signposts.

challenges.challenge: Coverage of 252.6% is the FY2025 bank-only ratio (F16, S3). The 9M26 ex-BSI ratio is 235% (F24: 'gross NPL remained stable at 1.02%, with steady NPL coverage at 235%'), and the report cites [S3][S2] for 252.6% in both §3 and §5. The buffer it uses to argue the 6.76% loans-at-risk book is 'adequate' fell by 18pp while LaR rose 93bp QoQ. The report is describing the current book with last year's, better, coverage number.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Coverage is now stated as 235.0% at 9M26 everywhere the current book is assessed, and the report says explicitly that it has fallen from the 252.6% FY2025 bank-only figure, which is what the previous version obscured. F45 was added for the 9M26 ratio with a verbatim quote from S2 p.11.

challenges.challenge: The bull case adds -0.60pp to credit cost, taking it to 0.05% in FY2026E, 0.08% in FY2027E and 0.10% thereafter. The bank reported 0.60% in FY2025 and 0.63% in 9M26 and guides 0.6-0.8%. A 5-10bp through-cycle credit cost is outside anything the company has ever reported and below the guidance floor by 55bp; the bear's 1.25% is only 45bp above the guidance high. The bull is therefore farther from the evidence than the bear, yet it carries 25% probability and contributes about Rp540 per share (7% of the target) to the probability-weighted Rp8,006. The bull NIM of 4.85% and loan growth of 14% are likewise above the 4.5% and 11% guidance tops.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bull case now moves credit cost by only 5bp, to the 0.60% guidance floor, and caps the margin at the top of the maintained guidance range; the loan-growth shock is removed. The report states that the bull is constrained by evidence and that the bear has no such floor, which is why the tails are not symmetric in size. The asymmetry is justified in qc_justifications with sources.

challenges.challenge: The report states 'A free float of 37.3% keeps the shares liquid, and an insider holding of 54.7%' and 'the Indonesia Investment Authority holds a further slice', all cited [S3]. A grep of S3 finds no 'free float' and no 37.3% or 54.7% ownership figure (the 37,3xx hits are unrelated balance-sheet numbers); the free-float figure in the model comes from the konglo registry with source 'S25', which is not in fund record at all. The ownership structure is a first-order governance input for an SOE, so an unsourced percentage is not cosmetic.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The free float and insider figures are removed; they came from the konglo registry source S25, which is not a registered source. Ownership is now sourced to the results deck register: government 52.0% through Danantara, INA 8.0% and foreign 26.6%, quoted verbatim from S2 p.4 as F46-F48.

challenges.challenge: The base case is below the observed run-rate. 9M26 PATMI was Rp45,534bn (S2), i.e. Rp60.7tn annualised, against the model's FY2026E np_parent of Rp58.35tn (-3.9%); provisions annualise to Rp10.4tn against the model's Rp11.67tn (+12%). On the like-for-like 9M25 pro-forma PATMI (Rp37,730bn, Rp50.3tn annualised) the model's FY2026E is +16%, but the report headlines '3.7% earnings per share growth' by comparing an ex-BSI FY2026E with the inclusive FY2025A base. The report is materially understating its own base case and giving the market credit it has not earned.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The report no longer headlines inclusive-base EPS growth. It states that the base case is just under four percent below the annualised 9M26 run-rate and why (provisioning above the run-rate and a flat margin), cites the 20.7% pro-forma 9M26 growth and the 7.26% year-to-date bank-only growth, and explains that it anchors on the year-to-date figure rather than the published year-on-year rate.

challenges.challenge: Terminal growth of 4.0% is set at the bottom of the range the report itself says applies (4.5-5.0% IDR terminal cap) and roughly half the 8.57% nominal GDP path implied by the house macro deck (5.29% real + 3.28% CPI). The model's own retention supports 4.24% (ROE 20.24% x 21% retained), so 4.0% is below what the base case can fund without any argued share loss. The value effect is not trivial: the sensitivity grid shows +1pp of terminal growth lifts the target from Rp7,858 to Rp8,441 (+7.4%). This is a conservative choice presented as a cap, with the basis cited to the annual report rather than a macro source.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Terminal growth is 4.2%, equal to the sustainable ROE times retention at the 79% payout, and the basis says so and cites the capital constraint rather than the annual report. The report states why the 8.57% nominal macro path is not fundable at this payout.

challenges.challenge: 'The shares turned over IDR651,082,088,548.4bn a day over the last three months' is a unit error of 1e9: the model's adtv_idr is 651,082,088,548 rupiah, i.e. Rp651bn a day. It is also cited [S8], which is a 2,958-character CNBC article on bank-only credit growth and contains no turnover or 52-week price data; the Rp3,360-5,375 range is from S0.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The turnover placeholder now uses the bn filter and renders IDR651.1bn a day, and the turnover and 52-week range are cited to S0, which carries them, rather than to S8, which does not.

challenges.challenge: 'A one-point move in the cost of equity or in terminal growth changes the value by more than a change in either the margin or the credit charge' is contradicted by the model's own sensitivity grid: the +/-0.6pp NIM span is Rp6,726-8,965 (+/-1,106), the +/-0.6pp credit-cost span is Rp7,004-8,698 (+/-844), the +/-1pp COE span is Rp7,407-8,441 (+/-517) and the +/-1pp g span is Rp6,943-9,042 (+/-1,050). The operating levers dominate the COE lever, so the conclusion that 'the call is therefore a bet on the discount rate normalising as much as on the earnings' understates the operating risk in the call.
